Vulnerable @hypequery/clickhouse (<2.0.2) package install for CVE-2026-54658 AIWeaponization High
Surfaces hosts/containers where the vulnerable @hypequery/clickhouse npm package is present, either via file writes into node_modules/@hypequery/clickhouse or Defender TVM vulnerability inventory for CVE-2026-54658. This is the attack-surface pivot: SQL injection in escapeValue() is only exploitable where versions prior to 2.0.2 are deployed. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable package path (node_modules/@hypequery/clickhouse) and the CVE id from the GHSA advisory; NVD/cve.threatint confirm vulnerable versions <2.0.2. Package presence is the necessary precondition for any exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54658 • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstations that legitimately use @hypequery/clickhouse in dev but not exposed to untrusted input
  • CI/CD build agents restoring node_modules from cache before an upgrade PR lands
  • Security researchers cloning the vulnerable repo for testing
  • Container base-image rebuilds that reinstall the same version pending a patch
  • Internal analytics services already scheduled for the 2.0.2 upgrade
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","node")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installed SoftwareVersion is <2.0.2 and whether the service passes user-controlled input into hypequery query parameters (check exposure vs. internal-only). 2) Contain: prioritise upgrade to 2.0.2+; for internet-facing services, gate the endpoint behind a WAF rule blocking backslash-quote sequences until patched (do NOT rely on app-side input sanitisation — advisory says the library must fix escaping). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC-2/UC-3 to check whether any exploitation attempts (backslash-quote payloads) already hit this host, and inventory all other hosts/images carrying the package.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"node_modules\@hypequery\clickhouse" or FolderPath has "node_modules/@hypequery/clickhouse"
| where FileName =~ "package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), SampleFolder=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId == "CVE-2026-54658" or (SoftwareVendor has "hypequery" and SoftwareName has "clickhouse")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Vulnerable @hypequery/clickhouse npm package file write (CVE-2026-54658)
id: 6f2a1c84-3d9e-4b7a-9f01-2c6b5e8a1d44
description: Detects installation/presence of the CVE-2026-54658 vulnerable @hypequery/clickhouse package via file writes under node_modules.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54658
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:

logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains|all:
      - 'node_modules'
      - '@hypequery'
      - 'clickhouse'
  condition: selection
level: medium
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/node_modules[\\/]@hypequery[\\/]clickhouse/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*node_modules*hypequery*clickhouse*" by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*node_modules*hypequery*clickhouse*" by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
CVE-2026-54658 SQL injection: trailing backslash quote-escape payload in web/proxy request parameters AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the specific exploitation primitive from CVE-2026-54658 — a parameter value using a trailing backslash to escape the closing single quote (\') followed by injected SQL — inside HTTP request query strings captured by WAF/proxy or web-tier logs. This is the on-the-wire signature of the escapeValue() bypass, not a generic SQLi template. Rationale: Targets the advisory's exact mechanism — 'a trailing backslash to escape the closing quote' — as the \'(-encoded %5c%27) sequence immediately preceding SQL keywords, which is far more specific than generic OR-1=1 SQLi. Payloads in POST/JSON/gRPC bodies won't appear in URL query strings (noted limitation); pair with UC-3 for backend confirmation. Defender endpoint telemetry has no HTTP request-parameter source, so defender_kql is intentionally blank. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54658 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate URLs containing Windows file paths that end in a backslash before a quoted token
  • Security scanners (Burp/ZAP/Nuclei) running authorized SQLi test suites against the app
  • Regex-heavy application parameters that naturally contain 'or'/'select' substrings adjacent to escaped characters
  • Marketing/analytics query strings with URL-encoded punctuation that coincidentally matches
  • WAF already blocking and re-logging the same payload multiple times per request
Suppression filter
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(union(%20|\+|\s)+select|;(%20|\+|\s)*(drop|insert|update|delete)|--|/\*)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the RequestURL, confirm the \'-then-SQL structure targets a hypequery-backed endpoint, and check the source IP's request history for enumeration/fuzzing bursts. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, add a rule rejecting backslash-immediately-before-quote in parameters, and confirm the target service is on @hypequery/clickhouse 2.0.2+. 3) Hunt: correlate the request timestamp against UC-3 ClickHouse query-log/syntax-error events on the backend, and review DB audit logs for successful UNION/stacked queries or data reads following the request.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(%5c|\\)(%27|')(?:%20|\+|\s)*(or|union|select|and|;|--|%3b)"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*%5c%27*" OR Web.url="*%5C%27*" OR Web.url="*%5c%2527*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_method, Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | regex url="(?i)(%5c|\\)(%27|')(?:%20|\+|\s)*(or|union|select|and|;|--|%3b)" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*%5c%27*" OR Web.url="*%5C%27*" OR Web.url="*%5c%2527*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_method, Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | regex url="(?i)(%5c|\\)(%27|')(?:%20|\+|\s)*(or|union|select|and|;|--|%3b)" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Vulnerable goshs exposure: process launched with --webdav and --no-delete (<= v2.1.3)

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] WebDAV MOVE succeeds (201/204) against goshs --no-delete server · [LLM] WebDAV --no-delete probe: 403 DELETE then successful MOVE on same path · [LLM] WebDAV MOVE with Overwrite:T header (destructive RemoveAll on destination)

goshs running --no-delete deletes/renames files on disk (CVE-2026-64863 MOVE bypass) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual data-loss primitive: a goshs process launched with the --no-delete guard that nonetheless performs file rename/delete operations on disk. Under the CVE, a WebDAV MOVE renames (deletes) the source and, with Overwrite:T, RemoveAll's the destination — so any FileDeleted/FileRenamed initiated by a goshs '--no-delete' instance is the bypass executing. Rationale: Binds the two article-specific strings that together prove exploitation: the process image 'goshs' AND the '--no-delete' flag it was launched with, correlated to an actual FileDeleted/FileRenamed. A no-delete instance deleting files is the CVE by definition — near-zero benign overlap.
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator legitimately using the goshs UPLOAD or unrestricted mode (no --no-delete flag) — excluded by the cmdline filter
  • goshs writing/overwriting freshly uploaded files in an allowed upload dir (FileWritten, not delete)
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantining a file goshs just wrote, showing as a delete on the same path
  • Log-rotation or temp-file cleanup by a wrapper script that happens to share the goshs working dir
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--upload-only","-uo") and ActionType == "FileCreated")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the goshs cmdline actually contains --no-delete and identify the deleted/renamed FolderPath+PreviousFolderPath — a rename to an unrelated name or a delete of a served artifact confirms abuse. 2) Contain: stop the goshs service and block its listening WebDAV port at the host firewall; snapshot the served directory for recovery. 3) Hunt: pull the WebDAV access log for MOVE requests around the file event, extract source IPs, and search for the same client issuing PROPFIND enumeration or repeated MOVE calls across other goshs hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "goshs"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, PreviousFolderPath, FileName, PreviousFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where EventType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WebDAV MOVE succeeds (201/204) against goshs --no-delete server AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the wire-side signature of the bypass: a WebDAV MOVE verb returning 201 Created or 204 No Content. Under a correctly enforced --no-delete policy MOVE should be 403; a successful MOVE is the source-file deletion (rename) primitive the CVE exposes on the goshs WebDAV port. Rationale: Keys on the exact article verb+status: MOVE returning 201/204. Successful WebDAV MOVE is rare in most estates and is the documented deletion primitive; scoping to the goshs host (by DstIpAddr/port) turns it high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDAV clients (macOS Finder, Windows Explorer web folders, Cyberduck) that use MOVE for normal rename operations on an intended-writable share
  • A goshs instance intentionally run WITHOUT --no-delete where MOVE is expected
  • Backup or sync tooling that stages files via MOVE/rename over WebDAV
  • Automated CI artifact reorganisation against a non-protected goshs endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm DstIpAddr/port is a goshs --no-delete instance (check the host's process cmdline) and inspect the MOVE Url + Destination to see which served file was renamed away. 2) Contain: restrict the WebDAV port to trusted source IPs or take goshs offline until upgraded past v2.1.3. 3) Hunt: from the source IP, enumerate all MOVE/DELETE/PROPFIND to the same host and correlate to host-side FileDeleted events (see the goshs file-deletion UC) to confirm data loss.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "MOVE"
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (201, 204)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Successful WebDAV MOVE (goshs --no-delete Bypass CVE-2026-64863)

WebDAV --no-delete probe: 403 DELETE then successful MOVE on same path AIExploitation High
Detects the exploit's discovery-to-abuse pivot described verbatim in the advisory: DELETE is blocked (403) but MOVE on the same resource succeeds. Correlating a 403 DELETE followed within 60s by a 201/204 MOVE on the identical URL from the same client is the bypass signature. Rationale: Directly encodes the advisory's stated asymmetry ('DELETE is correctly blocked (403) but MOVE still destroys files') as a same-URL, same-client 403-DELETE→2xx-MOVE temporal correlation — an operational sequence with essentially no benign explanation.
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A WebDAV client that retries a failed delete as a rename by design (rare, but some sync tools fall back)
  • Two unrelated users hitting the same URL where one's DELETE is denied by ACL and another legitimately renames — mitigated by same-SrcIpAddr join
  • Load-balancer health probes issuing method variety (won't produce 403+2xx on same file path)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request sequence from SrcIpAddr to DstHostname — a 403 DELETE immediately followed by a 2xx MOVE on the same Url is a deliberate probe; note the Destination header target. 2) Contain: block SrcIpAddr at the WAF/proxy and restrict the goshs WebDAV port; preserve the served directory for recovery. 3) Hunt: sweep all goshs hosts for the same source IP and for host-side FileDeleted/FileRenamed by goshs to quantify data destroyed.
let win = 60s;
let moves = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where HttpMethod =~ "MOVE" and toint(HttpStatusCode) in (201,204)
    | project MoveTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "DELETE" and toint(HttpStatusCode) == 403
| project DelTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| join kind=inner moves on SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| where MoveTime between (DelTime .. DelTime + win)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', MoveTime, DelTime)
| project DelTime, MoveTime, DelaySec, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| order by MoveTime desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method IN ("DELETE","MOVE") by _time, Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.status span=1s | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval isDenyDelete=if(http_method="DELETE" AND status==403,1,0), isMove=if(http_method="MOVE" AND (status==201 OR status==204),1,0) | stats max(eval(if(isDenyDelete==1,_time,null()))) as delTime max(eval(if(isMove==1,_time,null()))) as moveTime values(status) as statuses by src, dest, url | where isnotnull(delTime) AND isnotnull(moveTime) AND moveTime>=delTime AND (moveTime-delTime)<=60 | eval delaySec=moveTime-delTime | sort - moveTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method IN ("DELETE","MOVE") by _time, Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.status span=1s | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval isDenyDelete=if(http_method="DELETE" AND status==403,1,0), isMove=if(http_method="MOVE" AND (status==201 OR status==204),1,0) | stats max(eval(if(isDenyDelete==1,_time,null()))) as delTime max(eval(if(isMove==1,_time,null()))) as moveTime values(status) as statuses by src, dest, url | where isnotnull(delTime) AND isnotnull(moveTime) AND moveTime>=delTime AND (moveTime-delTime)<=60 | eval delaySec=moveTime-delTime | sort - moveTime
WebDAV MOVE with Overwrite:T header (destructive RemoveAll on destination) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the second, more destructive bypass path: a WebDAV MOVE carrying the 'Overwrite: T' header, which makes golang.org/x/net/webdav RemoveAll the existing destination before renaming — clobbering a pre-existing victim file even under --no-delete. Requires WAF/proxy header capture. Rationale: Targets the exact header the advisory names as the overwrite mechanism ('with Overwrite: T it additionally performs an explicit RemoveAll on the destination'). MOVE+Overwrite:T is the destructive-clobber variant and is not a shape normal clients emit against a read-controlled share.
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • macOS Finder / Windows mini-redirector legitimately sending Overwrite:T on renames against an intentionally writable WebDAV share
  • Sync clients (Cyberduck, davfs2) that default Overwrite:T on rename
  • Proxy not capturing request headers → query silently returns nothing (coverage gap, not a benign hit)
  • A goshs instance run without --no-delete where overwrite is expected behaviour
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target DestinationHostName is a goshs --no-delete instance and read the Destination header to see which existing file was RemoveAll'd. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP and restrict the WebDAV port; recover the clobbered file from backup/snapshot. 3) Hunt: correlate to host-side FileDeleted+FileWritten to the same path by the goshs process, and search other goshs hosts for MOVE+Overwrite:T from the same client.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "MOVE"
| where Message has "Overwrite: T" or Message has "Overwrite:T" or DeviceCustomString1 has "Overwrite" or RequestContext has "Overwrite"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceCustomString1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable goshs exposure: process launched with --webdav and --no-delete (<= v2.1.3) AIWeaponization High
Inventory/exposure hunt for the vulnerable configuration itself: any goshs process started with both --webdav and --no-delete is exploitable by CVE-2026-64863 until upgraded past v2.1.3 (commit ba00ce3). Surfaces the attack surface before it is abused. Rationale: Uses the two flags the advisory names as the vulnerable combination (--webdav + --no-delete) plus the binary name goshs; projecting ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion lets an analyst confirm <= 2.1.3 without hand-editing the query.
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A goshs instance already upgraded past v2.1.3 where the flag combo is present but patched — check ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion
  • Internal-only goshs on a segmented network with no untrusted WebDAV clients (still vulnerable, lower priority)
  • Security team running goshs deliberately for a lab/CTF exercise
  • A renamed goshs binary — mitigated by also matching via the --no-delete/--webdav cmdline tokens
Suppression filter
| where ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion !in ("2.1.4","2.2.0") or isempty(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the goshs version (ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion / --version) is <= 2.1.3 and determine whether the WebDAV port is reachable from untrusted networks. 2) Contain: upgrade goshs past 2.1.3, or firewall the WebDAV port to trusted hosts as an interim control. 3) Hunt: for every exposed instance, review WebDAV access logs for MOVE/Overwrite:T activity and host-side goshs file deletions to determine if the bypass was already used.

| where ProcessCommandLine has "--webdav" and ProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--webdav" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs vulnerable SFTP config: -sftp with empty-credential -b and no keyfile (CVE-2026-62325) AIExploitation High
Hunts for the goshs process being started with the SFTP subsystem enabled and basic-auth (`-b`) containing an empty username or empty password segment while no keyfile (`-fkf`) is supplied. This exact combination causes gliderlabs/ssh to fall back to NoClientAuth=true, granting unauthenticated SFTP file access as described in the advisory. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact reproduction string `-b 'admin:' -sftp` with no `-fkf`: the regex catches both the empty-password (`admin:`) and empty-username (`:pass`) variants, and excluding `-fkf` isolates the vulnerable NoClientAuth path. Cross-checked GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm and the prior GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv it incompletely fixes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team/pentest engagement standing up goshs for quick file transfer
  • CTF or lab environment intentionally reproducing CVE-2026-62325
  • Security researcher validating the advisory PoC
  • DevOps engineer using goshs as an internal passwordless file drop behind a firewall
  • goshs started with a legit `-b user:pass` where the password happens to contain a trailing space (rare parsing edge)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pentest" and FolderPath !startswith "/opt/labs/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the goshs cmdline truly has an empty credential segment and no `-fkf`, and identify the listening port and whether the host is internet-facing. 2) Contain: kill the goshs process and block inbound to its SFTP port at the host/edge firewall; if internet-facing, treat any served files as exposed. 3) Hunt: pull inbound connections to that port and file read/write events by the goshs PID to scope what was accessed or planted, and search other hosts for the same vulnerable invocation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName has "goshs" or ProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-sftp" and ProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+([^\s:]+:(\s|$)|:[^\s]+)"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "goshs" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "-sftp" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+([^\s:]+:(\s|$)|:[^\s]+)"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs launched with empty-credential -b basic auth (empty user or pass segment) AIInstallation Medium
Broad hunt for any goshs invocation whose `-b` basic-auth argument has an empty username (`:pass`) or empty password (`user:`) segment without a keyfile, regardless of whether `-sftp` is present. Complements the combined-flag alert by catching the misconfiguration itself, including future input variants of the unfixed `&&` root cause. Rationale: Directly encodes the advisory's two exploitable input formats `-b 'admin:'` (empty password) and `-b ':pass'` (empty username) via a single regex, and excludes the `-fkf` keyfile flag whose presence installs a PublicKeyHandler and closes the NoClientAuth path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin deliberately running goshs with only a username for an internal HTTP share (SFTP not enabled)
  • Red-team tooling directory containing goshs test invocations
  • Automation/CI that spins up goshs with placeholder credentials for smoke tests
  • Documentation or training material commands captured by EDR shell logging
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-sftp" and DeviceName !startswith "lab-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether `-sftp` is also present (SFTP + empty cred = unauthenticated file access) versus HTTP-only, and check the host's exposure. 2) Contain: stop the process if SFTP is enabled or the host is internet-facing; otherwise flag the owner to add `-fkf` or full credentials. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same goshs binary and cmdline pattern and review file-transfer telemetry from any long-running instances.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName has "goshs" or ProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+([^\s:]+:(\s|$)|:[^\s]+)"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "goshs" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+([^\s:]+:(\s|$)|:[^\s]+)"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File read/write by goshs SFTP server process (post auth-bypass collection) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects file create/modify/delete/rename operations whose initiating process is a goshs instance running with `-sftp`. After the empty-credential bypass, the goshs process itself performs all SFTP file I/O, so its filesystem activity is the collection-phase signal of an attacker reading or planting files. Rationale: Because goshs serves the SFTP subsystem in-process, attributing file create/modify/delete events to a goshs process running with `-sftp` (the advisory's exploited mode) surfaces exactly the read/write/delete/rename impact the advisory lists, with no reliance on unconfirmed IOCs. Sigma omitted: this is a cross-table/aggregation detection, not single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1105

Anomalous Host header on Poweradmin OIDC/SAML/logout endpoints (CVE-2026-54588) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-54588 exploitation: requests to Poweradmin's /oidc/callback, SAML ACS/SLO, or /logout endpoints carrying an HTTP Host header value that has never been seen for that site in the 30-day baseline. Poweradmin embeds HTTP_HOST verbatim into the redirect_uri/ACS URL sent to the IdP, so an attacker-controlled Host value is the exploitation primitive. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable endpoints (/oidc/callback, SAML ACS/SLO, LogoutController) and the root-cause primitive (untrusted HTTP_HOST embedded in callback URLs). Baseline anti-join surfaces the attacker's poisoned Host (e.g. attacker.com) without hardcoding the victim's legit hostname. Cross-checked GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx and SentinelOne/NVD (CWE-20/601, CVSS 9.6). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-54588/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54588
ATT&CKT1190 T1656
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new vhost/hostname added to the Poweradmin front-end (rename, new DNS name, migration)
  • Uptime/health-check probes (Pingdom, StatusCake) that send synthetic Host headers
  • Load-balancer or Kubernetes ingress health probes hitting endpoints with pod-IP Host values
  • Vulnerability scanners run by the org's own security team (Nessus/Burp) sending crafted Host headers
  • CDN/WAF origin pulls that rewrite the Host to an internal origin name
Suppression filter
| where CsHost !in~ ("localhost","127.0.0.1") and CsHost !endswith ".internal" and CsHost !endswith ".svc.cluster.local" and not (CsUserAgent has_any ("Pingdom","StatusCake","kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests to the anomalous CsHost on the auth endpoints; confirm the Host value is not an owned domain and check whether the request produced a 301/302 to an IdP authorize URL (redirect_uri would contain the attacker host). 2) Contain: set interface.base_url in Poweradmin config/settings.php (activates the safe branch immediately) and upgrade to 4.2.4/4.3.3; fix the reverse proxy so it does not pass proxy_set_header Host $http_host. 3) Hunt: check the IdP for AADSTS50011 redirect_uri-mismatch events and any successful admin sign-ins in the hour that followed; audit PowerDNS zones (MX, SPF/DKIM, CAA, delegation) for unauthorized changes.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let RecentHours = 24h;
let AuthPaths = dynamic(["/oidc/","/saml","/logout"]);
let Baseline = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(LookbackDays) .. ago(RecentHours))
    | where CsUriStem has_any (AuthPaths)
    | summarize by CsHost;
AppServiceHTTPLogs

| where CsUriStem has_any (AuthPaths)
| where isnotempty(CsHost)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on CsHost
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Requests=count(), SampleUri=any(CsUriStem), SrcIPs=make_set(CIp,20), Statuses=make_set(ScStatus,10) by CsHost
| order by FirstSeen desc

Host header fuzzing burst against Poweradmin auth endpoints from single source AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects unauthenticated reconnaissance/injection probing for CVE-2026-54588: a single source IP hitting Poweradmin OIDC/SAML/logout endpoints with 2+ distinct HTTP Host header values inside a 10-minute window. This is the shape of an attacker enumerating which flow reflects HTTP_HOST into the outbound redirect_uri. Rationale: Self-contained fan-out on the article's specific auth endpoints; multiple distinct Host headers from one IP is the unambiguous signature of host-header injection probing described in the advisory (unauthenticated, no credentials required). No allowlist/placeholder needed. Thresholds (2 hosts, 3 requests) are conservative and self-evident from the attack shape. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-54588/

Spike of AADSTS50011 redirect_uri mismatch at IdP (poisoned Poweradmin callback) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the IdP-side footprint of CVE-2026-54588 when the OIDC/SAML IdP is Entra ID: a burst of AADSTS50011 (redirect_uri / reply-URL mismatch) failures on a single application within an hour. Entra rejects the attacker-poisoned redirect_uri (attacker.com/oidc/callback) because it is not a registered reply URL, so a cluster of 50011 on the Poweradmin app is high-fidelity evidence of active redirect_uri poisoning. Rationale: Directly maps the article's exploitation mechanic (poisoned redirect_uri sent to the IdP) to the IdP error it produces. Corroborated by Microsoft Learn / SSOJet: AADSTS50011 'spiking on URIs you never deployed' is the documented signature of an attacker probing crafted redirect_uri values — exactly this CVE. 5/hr threshold separates probing from a single stray config typo. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts50011-redirect-uri-mismatch • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx
ATT&CKT1528 T1190
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine app-registration reply-URL misconfiguration after a Poweradmin upgrade or hostname change
  • A single trailing-slash / http-vs-https typo in the app's configured base_url producing repeated 50011 for legit users
  • Developer/staging instance of Poweradmin pointed at the production app registration
  • Reply-URL propagation lag (~60s) right after an admin edits the app registration
  • Load-balanced deployment where one node has a stale/incorrect base_url
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIPs has_any ("10.","192.168.") and Users == 1)
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the failing redirect_uri/reply-URL values in the sign-in detail — legit misconfig repeats one owned URL, an attack shows external/attacker hostnames or many distinct URIs. 2) Contain: if attacker hosts are present, treat affected users as at-risk (revoke sessions/refresh tokens for any who authenticated), lock the app to strict reply-URL matching, and force Poweradmin's interface.base_url + patch. 3) Hunt: pivot to successful sign-ins for the same users from new IPs in the following hour (see companion UC), and audit PowerDNS zones for MX/SPF/DKIM/CAA tampering.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 50011   // AADSTS50011 redirect_uri / reply-URL mismatch
| summarize AttemptCount=count(), Users=dcount(AccountUpn), UserList=make_set(AccountUpn,20), SrcIPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by Application, ApplicationId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where AttemptCount >= 5   // 5+ reply-URL mismatches/hr on one app = probing, not a one-off config typo
| order by AttemptCount desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50011"
| summarize AttemptCount=count(), Users=dcount(UserPrincipalName), UserList=make_set(UserPrincipalName,20), SrcIPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by AppDisplayName, AppId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where AttemptCount >= 5
| order by AttemptCount desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:50011
CLOUD

| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`

Victim account takeover: new-IP sign-in within 1h of redirect_uri mismatch (CVE-2026-54588) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates the two halves of a successful CVE-2026-54588 account takeover on Entra: a successful sign-in for a user from an IP absent from their 90-day baseline, occurring within one hour of an AADSTS50011 redirect_uri-mismatch event for that same user. Catches the case where the attacker captured the victim's authorization code via a poisoned redirect_uri and then used it/logged in. Rationale: Implements reviewer suggestion #1 and ties the article's stated outcome ('IdP redirects the victim's authorization code to an attacker' → full account takeover, no credentials) to observable telemetry: a fresh-IP success closely following a 50011 for the same user. Baseline anti-join + 1h temporal window is high-fidelity and article-specific to the redirect-poisoning flow. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts50011-redirect-uri-mismatch
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User travels / switches to a new mobile-carrier or home IP the same hour a legit 50011 config error fired
  • VPN or corporate-proxy egress-IP rotation introducing a 'new' IP for an existing user
  • New device enrollment where the user re-auths from an unfamiliar network after an app-registration reply-URL fix
  • Roaming user behind CGNAT whose apparent IP changes between the failure and the success
  • Admin testing the app registration (deliberately triggering 50011) then logging in from a lab network
Suppression filter
| where DelayMin <= 60 and NewIP !startswith "10." and NewIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the success IP's geo/ASN vs the user's baseline and whether the 50011 FailIP differs; check what the session did next (consent grants, PowerDNS zone edits, mail-flow rules). 2) Contain: revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens, force password reset + re-MFA, and block the new IP; if the user is a Poweradmin admin, freeze PowerDNS zone changes. 3) Hunt: review PowerDNS for MX hijack, SPF/DKIM additions, CAA removals and subdomain delegation; sweep other users for the same 50011→new-IP pattern and confirm the app is patched (4.2.4/4.3.3) with interface.base_url set.
let Lookback = 7d;
let WindowHours = 1h;
let BaselineDays = 90d;
let UserIpBaseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(Lookback))
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | summarize by AccountUpn, IPAddress;
let RedirectFailures = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where ErrorCode == 50011
    | project FailTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, FailIP = IPAddress, Application;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| join kind=leftanti UserIpBaseline on AccountUpn, IPAddress
| join kind=inner RedirectFailures on AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowHours)
| project SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, NewIP = IPAddress, Country, Application, FailTime, FailIP, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, FailTime)
| order by SuccessTime desc
let Lookback = 7d;
let WindowHours = 1h;
let BaselineDays = 90d;
let UserIpBaseline = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(Lookback))
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
let RedirectFailures = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where ResultType == "50011"
    | project FailTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, FailIP = IPAddress, AppDisplayName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ResultType == "0"
| join kind=leftanti UserIpBaseline on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| join kind=inner RedirectFailures on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowHours)
| project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, NewIP = IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, FailTime, FailIP, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, FailTime)
| order by SuccessTime desc

Inbound QR-code PDF phishing lure delivery (UAT-11764 Australian campaign) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound, delivered emails carrying a single PDF attachment from an external sender — the auto-generated, victim-tailored QR-code lure UAT-11764 uses to bypass email gateways. Email gateways cannot read the QR-embedded URL, so the PDF attachment shape itself is the pivot. Rationale: Uses the article's specific delivery shape: single-PDF-attachment, zero-URL, inbound-delivered emails from external senders (QR code is inside the PDF, invisible to URL scanners). Volume-based fan-out per sender surfaces the auto-generated propagation. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-oauth-device-code-phishing-m365-20260325-c/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1598.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor invoices/statements delivered as single PDF attachments from external partners
  • DocuSign/Adobe-style PDF workflow emails with no inline URL
  • HR/payroll PDFs from external providers
  • Newsletter or marketing PDFs from external mailing lists
  • External recruiters sending PDF job descriptions
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("docusign.net","adobe.com","echosign.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the flagged PDF in a sandbox and inspect for an embedded QR code that resolves to an M365 credential-harvesting page; check sender domain reputation and whether the same PDF hash hit multiple recipients. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine/soft-delete the message tenant-wide via Explorer, block the sender domain, and if any recipient scanned the QR, force-reset their credentials and revoke sessions. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC 'ARToken/UAT-11764 credential-harvesting infrastructure contact' for pamconj.com/workers.dev hits, and review recipients' mailboxes for newly created inbox rules.
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileType =~ "pdf" or FileName endswith ".pdf"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
    | where AttachmentCount == 1 and UrlCount == 0
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where SenderFromDomain != tostring(split(RecipientEmailAddress,"@")[1])
| summarize Recipients = dcount(RecipientEmailAddress), Subjects = make_set(Subject, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp)
          by SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, FileName
| where Recipients >= 1
| order by Recipients desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where FileType =~ "pdf" or FileName endswith ".pdf"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
    | where AttachmentCount == 1 and UrlCount == 0
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where SenderFromDomain != tostring(split(RecipientEmailAddress,"@")[1])
| summarize Recipients = dcount(RecipientEmailAddress), Subjects = make_set(Subject, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
          by SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, FileName
| where Recipients >= 1
| order by Recipients desc
Contact with UAT-11764 / ARToken credential-harvesting infrastructure AIDelivery High
Alerts on any host DNS-resolving or connecting to the named UAT-11764 / ARToken phishing infrastructure (pamconj.com subdomains, the Cloudflare Workers harvesting page). These are concrete, second-source-corroborated IOCs tied to the M365 credential-harvesting and device-code flows. Rationale: Straight IOC match on the article's pre-extracted domains (dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com, clear90489058903-document.workers.dev); corroborated by BleepingComputer/CSA ARToken coverage. Any resolution is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/artoken-phaas-exposes-eviltokens-microsoft-365-phishing-toolkit/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst detonating the lure in a lab that shares corporate DNS
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving IOC domains
  • Sandbox/proxy pre-fetching the URL from a quarantined email
  • Cloudflare Workers domain reuse after takedown pointing to benign parking
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify which user/device resolved the domain and whether it followed an inbound QR-PDF email; correlate to any M365 sign-in from the same user within 30 minutes. Step 2 (contain): Reset the user's credentials, revoke all refresh tokens/sessions, and block the domains at proxy/DNS. Step 3 (hunt): Check the user's mailbox for new inbox rules, SharePoint file staging, and outbound internal phishing; pivot to device-code sign-in UC for the same UPN.

OAuth device-code authentication anomaly (ARToken/EvilTokens MFA bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces successful M365 sign-ins completed via the OAuth device authorization grant — the flow ARToken/EvilTokens abuses to obtain tokens and PRTs without the password or an MFA challenge. Buckets device-code successes per user with the source IP/geo so analysts can spot the attacker completing the code from a foreign location. Rationale: Targets the article's stated bypass — 'bypass MFA through the OAuth device authorization flow rather than stealing passwords' — by parsing AuthenticationProcessingDetails for the device-code marker and profiling source geo per user. Corroborated by BleepingComputer/CSA ARToken reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/microsoft-365-phishing-panel-uses-oauth-device-code-flow/amp/ • https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-oauth-device-code-phishing-m365-20260325-c/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate onboarding of shared/kiosk devices, conference-room displays, or IoT via device code
  • Users signing into Azure CLI / PowerShell on headless servers using device code
  • Smart-TV or Teams Room device enrollment
  • Help-desk-assisted device provisioning
Suppression filter
| where not (Apps has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and array_length(Countries) == 1)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each device-code success, confirm the source IP/geo matches the user's baseline and that a genuine device enrollment was expected; inspect the app the token was issued for. Step 2 (contain): If unexpected, revoke the user's refresh tokens and PRTs, disable the account, and remove any attacker-registered devices. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to CloudAppEvents for token-backed mailbox/SharePoint access, new inbox rules, and BEC-style outbound mail from the same principal.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| extend Details = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where Details has "Device Code" or Details has "deviceCode"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize SignIns = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Countries = make_set(Country, 10), Apps = make_set(Application, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp)
          by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where array_length(Countries) >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| extend Details = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where Details has "Device Code" or Details has "deviceCode"
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize SignIns = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Locations = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion), 10), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
          by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where array_length(Locations) >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
Post-compromise M365 inbox-rule evasion + SharePoint lure staging (UAT-11764) AIInstallation Medium
Correlates attacker post-auth behaviour from UAT-11764: creation of mail-hiding inbox rules for defense evasion combined with SharePoint document staging used to host follow-on lures. Buckets per actor so a single compromised mailbox driving both actions rises above routine rule edits. Rationale: Encodes the article's exact post-compromise chain — 'creating email inbox rules for defense evasion, leveraging SharePoint to host malicious documents' — as a same-actor, 24h correlation of hide-rule creation with SharePoint/OneDrive file staging. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power users who legitimately auto-file mail to folders and upload docs the same day
  • Exec assistants managing a delegated mailbox and SharePoint libraries
  • Migration/onboarding tooling creating rules and staging files in bulk
  • Marketing users publishing SharePoint documents while tidying their inbox
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Review the inbox rule logic (does it hide security/IT-alert senders or auto-delete?) and the staged SharePoint file (external-shareable? credential-harvest content?); confirm the actor's sign-in was device-code or from anomalous geo. Step 2 (contain): Delete the malicious rule, revoke external sharing links, revoke the account's tokens, and reset credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate that mailbox's contact list for the next wave of recipients, and search outbound mail for internal phishing sent post-compromise.
let RuleActors = CloudAppEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
    | where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Deleted Items","Junk Email","Archive","MarkAsRead","MoveToFolder")
    | project RuleTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, RuleData = tostring(RawEventData);
RuleActors
| join kind=inner (
    CloudAppEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where Application has "SharePoint" or Application has "OneDrive"
    | where ActionType in ("FileUploaded","FileModified","SharingInvitationCreated","AnonymousLinkCreated")
    | project StageTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, ObjectName, StageAction = ActionType
  ) on AccountObjectId
| where abs(datetime_diff('hour', StageTime, RuleTime)) <= 24
| project RuleTime, StageTime, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, RuleData, ObjectName, StageAction
| order by RuleTime desc
let RuleActors = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
    | where Parameters has_any ("Deleted Items","Junk Email","Archive","MarkAsRead","MoveToFolder")
    | project RuleTime = TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Parameters;
RuleActors
| join kind=inner (
    OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where OfficeWorkload in ("SharePoint","OneDrive")
    | where Operation in ("FileUploaded","FileModified","SharingInvitationCreated","AnonymousLinkCreated")
    | project StageTime = TimeGenerated, UserId, SourceFileName, Operation
  ) on UserId
| where abs(datetime_diff('hour', StageTime, RuleTime)) <= 24
| project RuleTime, StageTime, UserId, ClientIP, Parameters, SourceFileName, Operation
| order by RuleTime desc
Trojanized MeshAgent SYSTEM-service backdoor (Sinobi ransomware) AIInstallation Medium
Detects MeshCentral MeshAgent being installed/run from non-standard locations or as a service — the covert SYSTEM-level auto-start backdoor Sinobi operators used as primary C2 over encrypted WSS. Focuses on the weaponized deployment shape, not legitimate signed MeshCentral in Program Files. Rationale: Article states Sinobi weaponized MeshAgent as a 'SYSTEM-level auto-start service' communicating over WSS. Detection anchors on the MeshCentral binary/product name plus abnormal install path or service/installer parentage — distinguishing weaponized from legitimate RMM. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1219 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSPs/IT that legitimately deploy MeshCentral but stage the agent in ProgramData
  • MeshCentral agent auto-update writing to a temp path
  • Security testing/red-team MeshAgent deployments
  • Portable MeshAgent run from a user Downloads folder by a sysadmin
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "meshagent.exe" and FolderPath has @"\Program Files\Mesh Agent\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether MeshCentral is a sanctioned RMM in this environment; inspect the agent's config/WSS destination and whether it runs as a SYSTEM auto-start service. Step 2 (contain): Stop and remove the service, block the C2 WSS endpoint, and isolate the host given ~3-day dwell before encryption. Step 3 (hunt): Look for follow-on RDP/WinRM lateral movement, ntds.dit access, malicious GPO logon scripts, and rclone staging across the domain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "meshagent"
   or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "MeshCentral"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("meshcentral","--meshServiceName","msh=","--installPath")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Public\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("services.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","msiexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "meshagent"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meshcentral","--meshServiceName","msh=","--installPath")
| where ParentProcessName in~ ("services.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","msiexec.exe")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\Temp\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Public\\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: MeshAgent Backdoor Execution From Non-Standard Path

Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployment (Warlock / Storm-2603) AIInstallation Medium
Detects installation/execution of the Zoho Assist Unattended Agent — the RMM Warlock (Storm-2603) operators deployed for keyboard-less, persistent remote control. Flags the agent binaries/service when spawned by a shell or installer rather than an interactive install. Rationale: Article names 'Zoho Assist Unattended Agent' deployed by Warlock/Storm-2603 for no-user remote control. Detection keys on the Zoho Assist unattended-agent binaries plus scripted/installer parentage, which separates attacker deployment from a user-initiated GUI install. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-storm-2603-exploits-CVE-2026-23760-to-stage-warlock-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/help-desk that legitimately uses Zoho Assist Unattended Agent for support
  • Software-deployment tooling (SCCM/Intune) pushing Zoho Assist via msiexec
  • MSP onboarding installing unattended agents fleet-wide
  • User re-installing Zoho Assist after an update
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Verify Zoho Assist is not a sanctioned support tool here; check whether the install had prior change-approval/MDM enrollment and what account initiated it. Step 2 (contain): Uninstall the unattended agent, block Zoho Assist gateway domains at the proxy, and isolate the host if unauthorized. Step 3 (hunt): Look for co-deployed RMM (MeshAgent), lateral RDP/WinRM, and pre-encryption staging; review other endpoints for the same agent.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has_any ("ZA_Access","ZA_Connect","ZohoURS","ZMAgent","Zaservice")
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ZOHO"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "Zoho Assist"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "Unattended" and ProcessCommandLine has "install")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","msiexec.exe","explorer.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ZA_Access","ZA_Connect","ZohoURS","ZMAgent","Zaservice")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has "Zoho Assist"
   or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "Unattended" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "install")
| where ParentProcessName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","msiexec.exe","explorer.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GPO logon-script execution delivering domain-wide ransomware (Sinobi) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects scripts/binaries launched via the Group Policy logon-script host (gpscript.exe) — the mechanism Sinobi operators used for rapid, domain-wide ransomware deployment. A gpscript.exe parent spawning interpreters or referencing encryption/exfil tooling is the pivot. Rationale: Article states Sinobi 'deployed the ransomware across the entire domain using a malicious GPO logon script.' gpscript.exe as parent is the concrete host-side artifact of GPO logon-script execution; the >=3-host fan-out flags domain-wide push and references the .SINOBI/rclone payloads named in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1484.001 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise GPO logon scripts (drive mapping, printer setup) that call cmd/powershell
  • Login-time software inventory or config-management scripts
  • Newly added benign logon script rolled out fleet-wide
  • Admin troubleshooting logon-script execution on a group of hosts
Suppression filter
| where not (Cmds has @"\\NETLOGON\\" and Cmds has_any ("net use","printer","MapDrive.ps1"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Retrieve the GPO and the referenced script from SYSVOL; inspect for encryption/exfil logic or obfuscation, and check who last modified the GPO. Step 2 (contain): Disable/unlink the malicious GPO, block the script from executing (application control), and isolate affected hosts before mass encryption. Step 3 (hunt): Review SYSVOL write events for the responsible account, hunt for the MeshAgent backdoor and rclone exfil, and check for .SINOBI file writes domain-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "gpscript.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (".ps1",".bat",".vbs",".SINOBI","rclone")
| summarize HostCount = dcount(DeviceName), Hosts = make_set(DeviceName, 25), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp)
          by FileName
| where HostCount >= 3
| order by HostCount desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName =~ "gpscript.exe"
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".ps1",".bat",".vbs",".SINOBI","rclone")
| summarize HostCount = dcount(DvcHostname), Hosts = make_set(DvcHostname, 25), Cmds = make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
          by ActingProcessName
| where HostCount >= 3
| order by HostCount desc

rclone data exfiltration staging (Sinobi pre-encryption) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects rclone execution used by Sinobi operators to stage/exfiltrate data before encryption, including renamed rclone identified by its distinctive cloud-transfer flags. Pairs the binary/flags with public network egress to raise fidelity. Rationale: Article names 'data exfiltration staging activity conducted via rclone.exe.' Detection matches both the named binary and rclone's signature flags (--multi-thread-streams/--transfers/--config with copy|sync|lsjson), catching renamed copies. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admins/backups using rclone legitimately to sync to sanctioned cloud storage
  • DevOps pipelines calling rclone for artifact transfer
  • Personal use of rclone by power users
  • Data-migration projects using rclone copy/sync
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","backup.exe") and FolderPath has @"\Program Files\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the rclone config/remote target and the source paths being copied (file shares, DB dumps?); confirm whether rclone is sanctioned on this host and account. Step 2 (contain): Kill the process, block the destination cloud endpoint at egress, and isolate the host given exfil typically precedes encryption. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with MeshAgent C2, GPO logon-script deployment, and .SINOBI encryption on the same or downstream hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rclone.exe"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--multi-thread-streams","--transfers ","--config "," lsjson ")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" copy "," sync "," lsjson ","--multi-thread-streams")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "rclone.exe"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--multi-thread-streams","--transfers ","--config ")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (" copy "," sync "," lsjson ","--multi-thread-streams")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Rclone Cloud Exfiltration Execution

Mass .SINOBI file encryption (Sinobi ransomware impact) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts when a single process rapidly writes/renames files to the .SINOBI extension — the terminal encryption artifact of Sinobi ransomware. Thresholded per host/process to fire on the encryption burst. Rationale: Article states the incident 'resulted in the encryption of systems with the .SINOBI file extension.' The extension is a concrete, unique IOC; per-process burst thresholding makes it high-fidelity, low-FP impact detection. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher storing sample ransomware artifacts on a host
  • Backup/replication of already-encrypted files from a prior incident
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies retaining the .SINOBI name
  • A single test file created during tabletop/IR exercises (mitigated by the >20 threshold)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the writing process and whether it originated from a GPO logon script or the MeshAgent backdoor; identify scope of affected hosts. Step 2 (contain): Isolate all encrypting hosts immediately, kill the process, disable the responsible GPO/service, and preserve ntds.dit/credential-reset scope. Step 3 (hunt): Trace back to initial access (RDP/WinRM with the cracked service account), review rclone exfil for double-extortion data theft, and enterprise-wide sweep for the .SINOBI extension and MeshAgent C2.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".SINOBI" or PreviousFileName endswith ".SINOBI"
| summarize FileCount = count(), Sample = make_set(FileName, 10), Folders = make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId
| where FileCount > 20     // 20 = burst threshold separating mass-encryption from a stray test file
| order by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".SINOBI" or TargetFileExtension =~ "SINOBI"
| summarize FileCount = count(), Sample = make_set(TargetFileName, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| where FileCount > 20     // 20 = mass-encryption burst threshold
| order by FileCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

NightLedger DLL search-order hijack: SspiCli.dll side-load via AppVShNotify.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the NightLedger loader, which masquerades as SspiCli.dll and abuses delay-loaded RPCRT4 imports of the legitimate signed AppVShNotify.exe to gain execution. Fires when SspiCli.dll is loaded from any path outside the Windows system directories, where the genuine module never lives. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact side-load pair (SspiCli.dll masquerade against AppVShNotify.exe). The genuine SspiCli.dll ships only in System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS, so any other load path is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against Check Point Research and Nextron Systems, which document the same DLL-sideloading infection chain for this actor. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/fast-and-furious-nimbus-manticore-operations-during-the-iranian-conflict/ • https://www.nextron-systems.com/2026/06/01/detecting-nimbus-manticore-and-their-sideloading-infection-chains/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nimbus-manticore-deploys-nightledger.html
ATT&CKT1574.001 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party software that ships a private copy of SspiCli.dll in its install directory (rare but possible with older redistributables)
  • Application-virtualization test/staging deployments copying App-V binaries to non-standard folders
  • Software-packaging tools (e.g. App-V sequencer) that stage system DLLs to a working directory
  • Backup/restore utilities re-creating DLLs into shadow/temp paths
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName == "Microsoft Corporation" and FolderPath startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Application Virtualization")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the loaded DLL's SHA256/MD5 and signer; confirm it is unsigned or not Microsoft-signed and that the hosting process is AppVShNotify.exe. Check the folder for a co-located AppVShNotify.exe (attacker-planted). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the AppVShNotify.exe process tree, and quarantine the rogue SspiCli.dll. 3) Hunt: on the same host and peers, query for the mutex A8215357-F99A-44FE-BC65-D8F0434B0C03, outbound HTTPS to realhealthshop.com / tjconsultingservices.com, and reads of C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "SspiCli.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| extend SideloadHost = InitiatingProcessFileName
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SideloadHost, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FileName, LoadedDllPath = FolderPath, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 7
| where EventData has "SspiCli.dll"
| where EventData !has @"C:\Windows\System32" and EventData !has @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" and EventData !has @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, RenderedDescription
